newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy to send troops to Naples as mob war rages.
newsitem.headline: Italy to send troops to Naples as mob war rages.

text.p: Italy plans to send soldiers to the crime-ridden southern port city of Naples later this month to help police battle a wave of mob violence which has swept the area since the start of the year.

Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano told reporters on Monday that the troops would take over routine guard duties around the city, allowing hundreds of extra police officers to be redeployed in the battle against organised crime.
Napolitano said on Sunday that the centre-left government would decide this week on the exact nature of the planned operation, stressing it would be "limited and targeted".
Some 85 people have been killed and dozens injured over the past six months as the Naples Mafia, known as the Camorra, wages a ruthless war for supremacy within the fragmented organisation.

The feuding has often spilt over into the streets and there was public outrage last month after a young woman, walking home with her six-year-old son, was killed by a stray bullet during a mob attack in central Naples.

The decision to call in the army came after another weekend of terror, in which two suspected mobsters were mown down in broad daylight and a number of innocent bystanders, including an eight-year old girl, were injured in wild shootings.
Interior ministry officials said that around 600 troops would be drafted into the area to help restore order to a city which has been branded "the wild west" by Italian media.
But Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta said many more soldiers might be needed.
"It is not just a question of 600 soldiers because you have to think about shifts, so that number will have to be multiplied by at least three," he told reporters.
Naples is one of Europe's poorest cities and suffers chronic unemployment, but it has enjoyed a revivial in recent years and its newly restored historic centre has become a tourist draw.
Local hoteliers said they were worried that the sight of armed soldiers in the city might frighten visitors away.
"The presence of the army on the streets could damage Naples' image," said Mario Pagliari, head of the Naples hoteliers association.
But local politicians breathed a sigh of relief over the government's decision. "It is a useful, positive and important step," mayor Antonio Bassolino told reporters.

Napolitano said recent police successes against the 40 Camorra clans in and around Naples helped spark the internecine battles as depleted groups struggled for dominance. However, he cautioned that the army alone could not solve the problem.
"Unfortunately this is not an instant remedy. It is necessary to mobilize public opinion, to isolate the Camorra groups which fight each other ferociously," Napolitano said.
It is not the first time Italy has decided to send troops onto the streets.

The army was called up in 1978 following the kidnap and murder of the then prime minister Aldo Moro and, more recently, soldiers were sent to the southern region of Calabria and the island of Sardinia to help combat crime waves.
Troops are still stationed in Sicily five years after they were called in following the murder of two leading magistrates.
